0.title: Saved Not by Them but for Them
0.essay:
Few phrases make Christians more uneasy than “good works”. Say them too loudly and you sound as if you are trying to earn your way to heaven. Say them too quietly and faith shrinks into a private feeling. The New Testament says them often, and without embarrassment.

Two ditches

There is a ditch on each side of the road. In one, good works become a ladder we climb to reach God. That ends in pride for those who think they are climbing well, and despair for those who know they are not. In the other, grace becomes a reason to do nothing in particular. Paul shuts both ditches in three verses. “For by grace you have been saved through faith … not a result of works” (Ephesians 2:8–9), he says, and in the very next breath he adds that we are “created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10).

Not by them, but for them

That is the heart of this study. We are not saved by good works; we are saved for them. They are not the root of our life with God but its fruit. They do not buy his favour; they flow from it. Get the order right and good works become one of the gladdest things in the Christian life: a way of saying thank you, and of making the beauty of Christ visible on an ordinary street.

We will ask what makes a work good, how Paul and James fit together, why works matter, where the power for them comes from, what God does with our stained efforts, what rewards mean, and how all this looks on an ordinary weekday. The studies Assurance of Salvation, Union with Christ, Christian at Work and Fighting Sin & Temptation sit close by, and The Three Uses of the Law looks more closely at the law that gives our works their shape.

The one good worker

Underneath it all stands one person. Only one human being has ever done nothing but good works. “He went about doing good” (Acts 10:38), and at the end he could say to his Father, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). Our good works begin, continue and end in his.

The chapters

What Makes a Work Good?; Not the Root but the Fruit; Why Good Works Matter; Where Good Works Come From; Imperfect Works, Accepted in Christ; Rewards and the Judgment Seat; and Good Works in Ordinary Life.

For reflection

Which ditch do you tend to drift towards: good works as a ladder, or grace as a reason to coast? When you hear the words “good works”, what do you feel: guilt, suspicion, eagerness, or something else?

1.title: What Makes a Work Good?
1.essay:
We use the word “good” loosely: a good meal, a good film, a good deed. When the Bible speaks of good works it means something both humbler and higher than we expect. Humbler, because a cup of cold water can be one. Higher, because a work is measured not by how impressive it looks to us but by how it looks to God.

Source, rule and goal

Reformed teaching has long described a good work by three marks. The Heidelberg Catechism (Question 91) and the Westminster and 1689 Confessions (chapter 16) put it in much the same way: a good work is done from true faith, according to God’s word, and for God’s glory. There is a source, a rule and a goal.

From faith

First, the source. “Without faith it is impossible to please him” (Hebrews 11:6). Paul states a principle that reaches beyond the question about food he was answering: “whatever does not proceed from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23). A work is not only an outward act; it has a heart. Two people may give the same gift. One gives as a child who trusts and loves the Father. The other gives to buy a reputation, to quiet a conscience or to put God in his debt. God sees the difference. That is why Jesus warns against practising righteousness “before other people in order to be seen by them” (Matthew 6:1). The same coins can be worship or a performance.

By his word

Second, the rule. A good work is one God has asked for, not one we have invented to impress him. Jesus rebuked those who honoured God with their own traditions, “teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Matthew 15:9). In the late medieval church ordinary believers were often taught that pilgrimages, vows and the purchase of indulgences were especially pleasing to God, while the daily work of a farmer or a mother counted for little. The Reformers asked a simple question: has God asked for this? The Confessions say that good works are only those God commands in his word, not those devised by human zeal, however well meant.

That is freeing. Scripture is enough to make us “complete, equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:17). We do not need to hunt for exotic ways of pleasing God. A mother changing a nappy with a thankful heart is doing a good work. A self-chosen ordeal that God never asked for may be no good work at all.

For his glory

Third, the goal. “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). A good work aims beyond itself. It is not finally for my reputation, or even only for the result, good as the result may be. It is for God to be honoured as the giver of every good thing.

“Splendid vices”?

This raises a hard question. What about the kindness of people who do not believe? An atheist nurse sits through the night with a dying stranger. Is that not good? Augustine, reflecting in The City of God on the admired virtues of pagan Rome, argued that virtues not offered to God are in the end more like vices than true virtues. Later writers summed up his point in a phrase he never quite used: the virtues of the pagans are “splendid vices”.

We need to handle that phrase with care. Reformed teaching does not say that an unbeliever’s kindness is fake, or that it does no good. The Confessions grant that such deeds may be the very things God commands and may be of real use to others. They are often the fruit of God’s common grace, his kindness to all people, and Christians should honour them and thank God for them (the study Common Grace says more). The point is about what such deeds are before God. Done without faith and without aiming at his glory, they are missing their centre, like a beautiful wheel with no hub. They cannot become a ladder to heaven. Nor can ours.

Two small coins

Jesus once sat opposite the temple treasury and watched. The rich put in large sums. Then “a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny” (Mark 12:42). These were the lepton, the smallest coins in circulation. Jesus called his disciples over: “this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on” (Mark 12:43–44).

Some notice that Jesus had just condemned the scribes who “devour widows’ houses” (Mark 12:40), and hear sorrow in the scene as well as praise. Both may be true. But Jesus plainly honours her. Heaven’s arithmetic weighs the heart and the cost, not the sum. What no one else noticed, he noticed.

Ordinary callings

Martin Luther argued in his Treatise on Good Works (1520) that faith is the first and highest good work, and that the humblest task done in faith pleases God more than the grandest religious exercise done without it. The study Christian at Work follows this further.

A retired builder feels he has no good works left to offer. His knees are gone and he cannot help with church repairs any more. His pastor asks him what he does in an ordinary week. He rings two widowers every Sunday evening. He prays through the church list each morning. He sits with his wife through her dialysis. “Those are good works,” the pastor says. “God asked for every one of them.”

For reflection

Which of the three marks (faith, God’s word, God’s glory) do you find hardest to keep in view? How would you explain to a non-Christian friend why their kindness is real and yet cannot save them? What “two small coins” could you offer God this week that no one else will see?

2.title: Not the Root but the Fruit
2.essay:
An apple tree does not become an apple tree by producing apples. It produces apples because it already is one. Good works relate to salvation in much the same way. They are not the root that makes us God’s; they are the fruit that grows because we are.

Saved for good works

Ephesians 2 sets the order with great care. “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9). Works are shut out as the cause, so that no one in heaven will ever say, “I made the difference.” Then Paul goes on: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10).

The word for workmanship is the word for something made, a work of art. The great work in view is not ours but God’s: he has made us new. Good works are shut out as the root and welcomed as the purpose. We are not saved by them. We are saved for them.

The kindness of God appeared

Paul says the same to his co-worker Titus, left to lead the young churches on Crete. “He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5). Yet a few lines later he writes, “I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works” (Titus 3:8). The same apostle who will not let works anywhere near the root insists on them as fruit. In fact it is the mercy that produces them.

Where Christians differ: Rome and the Reformation

This was the heart of the sixteenth-century debate, and it should be stated fairly. The Roman Catholic Church, at the Council of Trent (in its decree on justification of 1547), taught that justification begins with grace that no one can merit. But it understood justification as more than forgiveness: it includes the inner renewal of the person. Good works done in that grace, Trent taught, truly increase justification and merit eternal life, because they are God’s gifts working in us. Catholics hold that this honours grace rather than human effort, and they rightly insist that grace really changes people.

The Reformers answered that Scripture uses “justify” for a verdict, not a process. God declares the ungodly righteous on the ground of Christ’s righteousness, counted to them and received by faith alone: “to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (Romans 4:5). Renewal is real, and it always comes with justification, but it is not its ground. John Calvin put the balance in a well-known line, paraphrased here: faith alone justifies, yet the faith that justifies is never alone.

This commentary’s view: justification is God’s once-for-all declaration that the believing sinner is righteous, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness counted to him and received by faith alone; no one can merit anything. This matters. If my works form any part of my standing before God, my standing is as unsteady as my works, and my works are very unsteady. If my standing rests on Christ, it is as firm as he is, and my works are set free to be what they were meant to be: thanks, not payment.

Paul and James

But does James not say the opposite? “You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone” (James 2:24). Paul says, “one is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:28). Luther once called James an epistle of straw beside Romans and John, though he later dropped the remark.

Read carefully, the two apostles are fighting different enemies. Paul opposes people who want to earn acceptance. James opposes people who claim a faith that changes nothing. The “faith” James attacks is bare agreement with facts: “Even the demons believe, and shudder!” (James 2:19). Such faith wishes a cold brother well and leaves him cold (James 2:15–16). James is asking how a living faith shows itself: “Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works” (James 2:18).

Notice which part of Abraham’s life each one uses. Paul quotes Genesis 15:6, where Abraham simply believed God’s promise and it was counted to him as righteousness. James points to Genesis 22, many years later, when Abraham offered Isaac. There, James says, “faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works” (James 2:22). In James, to be justified by works means to be shown to be righteous, proved genuine before the watching world. Paul tells us how a sinner is accepted. James tells us how to recognise the faith that receives it. Even Rahab showed her new trust in Israel’s God by hiding the spies at the risk of her life (James 2:25).

Accepted, therefore

Timothy Keller often pointed out that religion runs on the principle I obey, therefore I am accepted, while the gospel runs on I am accepted, therefore I obey. From outside they look the same. Underneath, one obeys from fear to get something from God; the other obeys from joy, because it has already been given everything.

A woman raised in a strict church spent thirty years trying to be good enough. She went to every meeting and volunteered for every rota, and she still lay awake wondering whether God was pleased with her. When she finally understood that she was accepted in Christ before she had done a thing, she expected to become lazy. Instead she found herself serving with a lightness she had never known. Nothing had changed on the rota. Everything had changed underneath it.

For reflection

Why do you think Paul is so careful that “no one may boast”? How would you explain to a friend the difference between Paul’s “faith” and the “faith” James attacks? Are your good works more often payment or thanks? How can you tell?

3.title: Why Good Works Matter
3.essay:
If good works do not save us, why bother? The question is as old as the gospel. Paul heard it in his own day: “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?” (Romans 6:1). His answer is not “because you had better”. It is a set of reasons that all grow from grace itself.

Gratitude

The Heidelberg Catechism is arranged in three parts: our misery, our deliverance, and our gratitude. Strikingly, the Ten Commandments and the whole teaching on good works come in the third part. Question 86 asks the obvious question: since we have been delivered by grace alone through Christ, without any merit of our own, why must we still do good works? The answer, in substance, is that Christ, having redeemed us by his blood, is also renewing us by his Spirit into his image, so that with our whole lives we may show that we are thankful to God, and so that he may be praised through us. It adds that we may be assured of our faith by its fruits, and that our neighbours may be won to Christ by our godly living.

That is the first and deepest reason. Paul begs us to offer our whole selves to God “by the mercies of God” (Romans 12:1). Good works are a thank-you note written with a life. They are not the price of the gift; they are what love does when it has been given everything.

The glory of God

Jesus said, “let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). Shortly after, he warned against doing righteousness “in order to be seen by them” (Matthew 6:1). Is that a contradiction? No. The difference is the goal. In the first case people see, and the Father is praised. In the second case people see, and I am praised. Good works are meant to be windows, not mirrors. People should look through them and see God.

The good of our neighbour

God does not need our good works. He is not short of anything. But our neighbour is. Luther’s teaching is often summed up in the saying that God does not need your good works, but your neighbour does. Paul tells the former thief to work “so that he may have something to share with anyone in need” (Ephesians 4:28). John is blunt: “let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth” (1 John 3:18). The hungry are not fed by our sincere feelings about them.

Evidence of a living faith

The Westminster and 1689 Confessions call good works the fruits and evidences of a true and living faith. Jesus put it simply: “every healthy tree bears good fruit” (Matthew 7:17). That is why good works can steady our assurance, though they are never its first ground. We look first to Christ, then see with thanks what he is growing in us. The study Assurance of Salvation sets out that order with care.

Jesus also gives a sobering warning. On the last day many will say, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?” (Matthew 7:22). And he will answer, “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:22–23). Impressive works are no proof. The question is whether they spring from a real relationship with him.

Witness to the watching world

Peter wrote to Christians who were slandered by their neighbours. His strategy was not a publicity campaign. “Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation” (1 Peter 2:12). The early church grew in a hostile empire partly because Christians cared for the sick in times of plague and took in abandoned babies when others did not. Good works do not convert anyone; only the Spirit does that through the word. But they make the word credible. They show that the gospel is not only true but good.

The goal of the cross

Finally, good works matter because Christ died for them. He “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14). Holiness is not an optional extra on top of salvation. It is part of what salvation is for. Jesus did not die to leave us as we were, only forgiven. He died to make us like himself. To shrug at good works is to shrug at the purpose of the cross.

An example

A young accountant is the only Christian in his office. He never preaches at anyone. But he does not pad his expenses, he covers for a colleague whose child is in hospital, and he stays late to help a new graduate who is struggling. After a year the graduate asks him, half joking, why he is “so annoyingly decent”. That question opens a conversation about Jesus that lasts for months. The works did not save her. They opened the door for the word that did.

For reflection

Which of these reasons moves you most, and which have you neglected? How can you tell whether a good work is a window or a mirror? Who is the “neighbour” who needs your good works this week? Why is it wrong to call holiness an optional extra?

4.title: Where Good Works Come From
4.essay:
You cannot make fruit by straining. No branch has ever produced a grape by clenching its fists. If good works are fruit, the most important question is not how hard we try, though we must try, but where the life comes from.

Prepared beforehand

Look again at the end of Ephesians 2:10. We are created for good works “which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10). Before you were born, God had already prepared the works he would give you to do. Not only your salvation, but the shape of your obedience, was in his mind before time began.

That is a great relief. You do not have to invent the meaning of your life or strain to do something impressive. The works are already laid out, like a path cleared through a forest. Your task is to walk in them, one step at a time: the conversation, the meal, the honest day’s work, the apology, the gift. Many of them will look small. None of them is accidental.

In Christ

The source of good works is a person. “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me” (John 15:4). And then: “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Not “you can do less”. Nothing that God counts as fruit.

Every believer is joined to Christ by the Spirit through faith. His life flows into us as sap flows into a branch. Paul could say, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Good works are what happens when the life of Christ comes out through the hands of ordinary people. The study Union with Christ explains this union more fully.

By the Spirit

The prophets saw this coming. Through Ezekiel God promised, “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26), and “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27). The law written on stone could tell people what was good; it could not make them want it. The Spirit changes the wanting. That is why Paul speaks of the fruit of the Spirit, not the achievements of the believer: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). And it is why the faith that counts is “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

God works, and we work

Does this make us passive? Paul answers in one of the most remarkable sentences in the Bible: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

Notice three things. Paul says work out, not work for. The Philippians already have salvation; they are to live it out in every corner of life. Second, the reason they can work is that God is working. His work does not replace ours; it creates it. Third, God works both the willing and the doing. He does not only give us strength once we have decided; he moves the decision itself.

So it is not God doing half and us doing half. It is God doing all, and us doing all. Paul puts it this way about his own ministry: “I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10). Augustine prayed in his Confessions, “Give what you command, and command what you will.” That prayer famously troubled Pelagius, who thought it would make people lazy. It does the opposite. People who know that God gives what he commands are the ones who dare to attempt what he commands.

Two wrong turns

There are two ways to go wrong here. Some Christians, longing for victory, have been taught to “let go and let God”, as if holiness came by surrender alone and effort were a sign of unbelief. Others work hard at holiness with very little sense of grace, gritting their teeth and wondering why they are so tired. Scripture walks between the two. As this commentary says elsewhere, we work because he works; passivity is never commanded, and nothing good is ever done without him.

The ordinary means

How, in practice, do we stay close to the vine? Through the ordinary means God has given: his word read and preached, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people. We are told to “consider how to stir up one another to love and good works” (Hebrews 10:24). Good works are not usually grown alone. They grow in a body.

An example

A woman resolves to be kind to her difficult mother-in-law. For a month she grits her teeth through every visit, and fails every time. Exhausted, she begins a different pattern. Before each visit she reads a few verses about Christ’s patience with his own slow disciples, and prays honestly: “I cannot love her. You can. Love her through me.” The visits do not become easy. But slowly she notices a patience she did not manufacture. She is still working hard. She is no longer working alone.

For reflection

How does it change your day to know that God has prepared good works for you to walk in? Which wrong turn do you tend towards: passivity or grim self-effort? What does “work out” rather than “work for” mean for you? Which of the ordinary means of grace do you most need to use more?

5.title: Imperfect Works, Accepted in Christ
5.essay:
Every honest Christian knows this: even our best works are mixed. We pray with wandering minds. We give and enjoy being thanked. We serve, and part of us wants to be seen serving. If good works must be perfect to please God, none of ours ever has.

Stained

Isaiah, confessing the sins of his people, says, “all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment” (Isaiah 64:6). He does not say our sins only; he says our righteous deeds. The things we are proudest of carry a stain.

The Confessions speak with the same honesty. The 1689 Confession, following the Westminster Confession (chapter 16), says that our best works cannot merit pardon of sin, and that as they come from us they are defiled and mixed with so much weakness and imperfection that they could not stand the severity of God’s judgment. That is not gloom but realism. It guards us from pride in our goodness and from shock at our badness.

Yet pleasing to God

And yet Scripture says, again and again, that God is pleased with the good works of his people. Paul calls a gift sent to him “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18). Hebrews says that doing good and sharing are “sacrifices” that are “pleasing to God” (Hebrews 13:16). How can stained works please a holy God?

Peter gives the answer in three words. Believers are “a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:5). Through Jesus Christ. Our persons are accepted because of him, and so are our works. The Confession puts it tenderly: since believers themselves are accepted through Christ, their good works are also accepted in him. God does not pretend the works are flawless. Looking on them in his Son, he is pleased to accept and reward what is sincere, though it comes with many weaknesses. Calvin taught the same: just as God freely accepts the believer in Christ, he freely accepts the believer’s imperfect works, their faults covered by Christ’s purity.

The gold plate

The Old Testament gives a beautiful picture of this. The high priest wore a plate of pure gold on his turban, engraved “Holy to the LORD.” God said that Aaron “shall bear any guilt from the holy things that the people of Israel consecrate as their holy gifts” (Exodus 28:38). Even the people’s gifts to God carried guilt. So the high priest bore it, “that they may be accepted before the LORD” (Exodus 28:38).

Our great High Priest does the same. He takes our prayers, our service and our giving, with all their mixed motives, and carries their guilt himself. What reaches the Father has passed through his hands.

A father and his child

God says of his people, “I will spare them as a man spares his son who serves him” (Malachi 3:17). Think of a small child who makes breakfast in bed for her father. The toast is burnt. Tea has slopped into the saucer. The kitchen is a disaster. Does he say, “This is not up to standard”? No. He is delighted, because it is his child and it was done in love. The father who sees the mess also sees the heart, and he is the one who taught her to love.

That is how our heavenly Father receives the works of his children in Christ. This is no excuse for sloppiness: a child who loves her father will want to do better next time. But it is wonderful news for everyone who has ever looked at their efforts and thought, “That will never be good enough for God.” In Christ, it is.

Free from perfectionism

Many Christians are paralysed by this. They will not serve until their motives are pure. They will not share their faith until they can do it perfectly. They abandon good works halfway because they are not good enough. But if we wait for pure motives, we will never do anything. The gospel frees us to begin, with our motives as they are, and to bring them to Christ as we go.

Jesus taught his disciples to say, when they had done everything commanded, “We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty” (Luke 17:10). That keeps us humble. But the same Lord will say to his servants at the end, “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21). That keeps us hopeful. We do not earn the “well done”. He gives it, for his own sake. The study Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation explores this freedom more deeply.

For some believers, the sense of never being good enough becomes crushing: constant checking, endless confessing of the same thing, sleepless nights of self-accusation. If that is you, please speak to your pastor and ask for a biblical counsellor, through your church or an organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the United States or Biblical Counselling UK. A good counsellor will open God’s Word with you, which is sufficient for the care of the soul, and will also ask you to see your doctor, because body and soul affect one another. Medical treatment is no failure of faith. And if your self-accusation has turned into thoughts of ending your life, do not wait: tell someone today, and call the emergency services or a crisis line.

An example

A woman stops helping at the church’s parent and toddler group. “I only do it because I like being needed,” she tells a friend. “That isn’t a good work.” Her friend, an older believer, laughs gently. “If you wait until you only want to help for God’s glory, the toddlers will be grown up. Go back. Tell the Lord your motives are mixed, and ask him to purify them while you serve. He accepts your work in Christ, mess and all.” She goes back the next week.

For reflection

Which of your good works do you most suspect of mixed motives? What difference does “through Jesus Christ” make to how you see them? How does the picture of the gold plate help you? Is there a good work you have abandoned because it was not good enough?

6.title: Rewards and the Judgment Seat
6.essay:
The New Testament speaks about rewards far more than many Christians are comfortable with. Jesus promises them. Paul works for them. To some, it sounds like a back door for earning salvation. Read carefully, it is one more display of grace.

The judgment seat of Christ

Paul writes to believers: “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10). He includes himself.

Is that not a contradiction of justification? Jesus said that whoever believes “does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (John 5:24), and Paul says, “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Both are true. The question of condemnation has been settled at the cross, once for all. Believers will not be condemned. But their lives will still be revealed, and their works weighed and rewarded. The verdict is not in doubt; the commendation is still to come. The judgment of those who reject Christ is the subject of the study Judgment and Hell.

Gold or straw

Paul’s fullest picture is in 1 Corinthians 3. The foundation is Christ, and nothing can replace it. On it each builder builds “with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw” (1 Corinthians 3:12). Then the Day comes and “the fire will test what sort of work each one has done” (1 Corinthians 3:13). “If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:14–15).

Paul is speaking first about teachers and leaders who build up the church, but the principle reaches every believer. Work done from faith, by God’s word, for his glory is gold. Work done for show is straw. Notice that the fire tests the work, not the person. The one who builds with straw is still saved, like someone pulled from a burning house with nothing but his life. This passage has sometimes been used to support the doctrine of purgatory, but the fire here falls on a single Day and tests works; it does not purify souls over long ages.

Rewards of grace, not wages

How can there be rewards if no one merits anything? Paul has already explained: “to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due” (Romans 4:4). The rewards of the kingdom are not wages. They are gifts that God, in his generosity, ties to the works he himself prepared and enabled. Augustine said that when God crowns our merits, he crowns nothing but his own gifts. In the parable of the labourers, those hired at the last hour receive a full day’s pay, a denarius, and the owner asks the grumblers, “do you begrudge my generosity?” (Matthew 20:15).

Are rewards then mercenary? C. S. Lewis, in The Weight of Glory, answered that some rewards are not mercenary at all. A man who marries a woman for her money is mercenary. A man who marries her for love and finds that marriage is the reward of love is not. The rewards of heaven are like that: the natural fulfilment of loving God, above all the joy of God himself. “Your reward shall be very great” (Genesis 15:1), God told Abram, and then gave Abram himself.

So the promises are full of tenderness. A cup of cold water given to one of his disciples will “by no means lose his reward” (Matthew 10:42). “God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name” (Hebrews 6:10).

Where Christians differ: degrees of reward

Christians have understood rewards in several ways. Many Reformed and evangelical teachers have held that there are degrees of reward, pointing to the servants set over ten cities and over five (Luke 19:17–19) and to the builders of 1 Corinthians 3. Jonathan Edwards used the picture of vessels of different sizes all thrown into an ocean of joy: every one is full, though some hold more. Roman Catholic teaching links degrees of glory to merit. Some evangelical scholars, such as Craig Blomberg, have argued instead that the reward is eternal life itself, the same for all believers, and that talk of higher and lower places breeds a spiritual class system. Others, especially in the Free Grace movement, distinguish sharply between salvation, which can never be lost, and rewards such as reigning with Christ, which unfaithful believers can forfeit, and they read many warning passages this way.

This commentary’s view: Scripture does teach that rewards differ (Luke 19:17–19; 1 Corinthians 3:14–15), and that they are wholly of grace. There are no degrees of acceptance: every believer is welcomed on exactly the same ground, the righteousness of Christ. Capacities for joy may differ, but every vessel will be full, and there will be no envy and no pride in heaven. The redeemed will gladly “cast their crowns before the throne” (Revelation 4:10). The warning passages are not only about lost rewards; they are God’s real means of keeping his people. And the greatest reward of all is the same for every believer: God himself.

Living towards the Day

What difference should this make now? Paul says, “do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5). That warns the proud. It comforts the unseen.

An elderly woman prays for her neighbours every morning for forty years. No one knows. She raises a disabled son with no applause. On that Day, the Lord who “sees in secret” (Matthew 6:4) will speak her name and tell the whole creation what she did. Her reward will not be wages. It will be the delight of the Father who prepared every one of those works for her, and walked with her in them.

For reflection

How do you feel about standing before the judgment seat of Christ? Why is it not a threat to believers? What would building with gold rather than straw look like in your situation? Whose hidden faithfulness do you look forward to seeing honoured on that Day?

7.title: Good Works in Ordinary Life
7.essay:
Most good works do not look heroic. When Dorcas died, Luke tells us she had been “full of good works and acts of charity” (Acts 9:36). The evidence was a room full of weeping widows holding up the “tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them” (Acts 9:39). Her good works could be folded and worn.

At work

For most of us, most of our waking hours are spent working, paid or unpaid. Paul urges believers “to work with your hands … so that you may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one” (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12), and “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). An honest invoice, a properly mended pipe, a patient lesson with a struggling pupil: these are good works.

At home

Paul tells children and grandchildren “to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God” (1 Timothy 5:4). Changing a nappy, cooking the meal no one thanks you for, listening to a teenager at midnight, visiting an ageing parent who no longer remembers your name: God calls these pleasing.

One guard rail: kindness at home never means staying in danger. Where there is abuse, safety comes first. Get yourself and your children to safety, tell someone you trust, and report it to the authorities. Love does not require anyone to enable cruelty.

In the church

“So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians 6:10). The local church is the first place where good works are practised and received. Making tea, welcoming newcomers, teaching children, visiting the sick, giving, praying for the elders: all of these build with gold.

The neighbour and the poor

Paul’s “especially” never cancels his “everyone”. Jesus told the story of a Samaritan who stopped for a wounded stranger, and ended it, “You go, and do likewise” (Luke 10:37). Scripture says, “Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD” (Proverbs 19:17), and John asks how anyone who closes his heart to a brother in need can claim that God’s love abides in him (1 John 3:17).

Matthew 25 read carefully

Jesus’ picture of the sheep and the goats is one of the most searching passages in the Bible. The King says to those on his right, “I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35), and adds, “as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).

Two things need care. First, who are “the least of these my brothers”? Many read them as all the poor and suffering. This commentary thinks they are most likely Christ’s needy disciples, since in Matthew Jesus calls those who do his Father’s will his brothers (Matthew 12:49–50), and promises a reward to anyone who gives a cup of water to “one of these little ones” because he is a disciple (Matthew 10:42). Yet either way, Scripture plainly commands care for all the poor, and no Christian can use this reading to walk past anyone.

Second, the sheep are not earning anything. They are astonished: “Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you?” (Matthew 25:37). They kept no record. And their inheritance was “prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34), long before they gave anyone a meal. Their works did not make them the King’s; they showed that they were. That is the whole of this study in one scene.

How to begin

Begin each day by asking God to show you the works he has prepared, then look at the people in front of you: they are usually the answer. Give some things in secret, so that your left hand does not know what your right hand is doing (Matthew 6:3). Set aside money for giving before you spend. Ask your church where help is needed, rather than inventing heroic projects. Do the next good thing, not the hundredth. And rest. Jesus told his tired disciples, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while” (Mark 6:31). A worn-out servant is no proof of holiness.

When it all feels fruitless, remember the promise: “let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9).

A nurse with three children comes home from a twelve-hour shift and wonders whether she has done anything for God that day. She has. She calmed a frightened old man before surgery, caught a medication error, listened to a grieving colleague, and still read her daughter a bedtime story. None of it felt holy. All of it was prepared by God, accepted in Christ, and seen by her Father.

The one truly good worker

In the last week of his life a woman poured costly ointment over Jesus’ head, and people grumbled at the waste. Jesus said, “She has done a beautiful thing to me” (Mark 14:6). The words translate the very phrase the New Testament uses for a good work: literally, she has worked a beautiful work. Then he went out to do the most beautiful work ever done.

Here is the one human being whose works were never stained. The crowds said of him, “He has done all things well” (Mark 7:37). He kept the law in thought, word and deed, from the manger to the cross, and he did it for us. On the cross he finished the work no one else could do, and cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30). His good works are the only ones that save, and they are counted to everyone who trusts him. Our good works are the overflow of his. At the end of the Bible the bride of Christ is dressed for the wedding in fine linen, “the righteous deeds of the saints” (Revelation 19:8). Yet even that linen, John says, “was granted her” (Revelation 19:8). From first to last, our good works are his gift.

So we work, and we rest, and we wait for him, praying with Hebrews that the God of peace will “equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Hebrews 13:21).

For reflection

Where in your ordinary week are the good works God has prepared for you? Who are the poor or needy whom God has put in your path? How does the surprise of the sheep in Matthew 25 free you from keeping score? What does it mean to you that Christ’s good work, not yours, is the one that saves?
